chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Husayn ibn Nu'aym, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who designated a house as a residence for a man for the days of his life, or designated it for him and his descendants after him. I asked: Is it for him and his descendants as stipulated? He said: 'Yes.'

I said: If he needs [money], can he sell it? He said: 'Yes.' I said: Does his sale of the house break the residence right? He said: No, the sale does not break the residence right. Thus, I heard my father (peace be upon him) say, that Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Sale does not break lease/residence, nor does residence break sale. But he sells it on the condition that the buyer does not possess what he bought until the residence period expires as stipulated. And so is the case with lease.'

I said: If he returns to the lessee his money and all that was incumbent upon him regarding maintenance and upkeep for what he leased? He said: 'Provided it is with good will and the lessee is pleased with that, there is no objection.'

key_terms.السُّكْنَى: Life tenancy or right of residence for a specific period

ai.seo_question: Does selling a property invalidate the existing life tenancy (sukna) or lease rights of the occupant?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between ownership and usufruct, establishing that a sale of property does not extinguish the pre-existing right of 'sukna' (life tenancy) or 'ijarah' (lease). It further specifies that while the buyer acquires the title, their possession is conditional upon the tenant's stay, and early termination requires mutual consent and fair compensation for maintenance, reflecting the Shia emphasis on contractual integrity and the protection of the weaker party's rights.
